name: Mutual Assured Destruction
statement: If both sides can annihilate each other even after being struck first, neither dares strike at all.
meaning: Mutual assured destruction is a doctrine in which a full-scale use of nuclear weapons by two or more opposing sides would completely annihilate both the attacker and the defender. Its condition is that both sides hold an assured second-strike capability, the power to retaliate devastatingly even after absorbing a first strike, so that neither has any rational incentive to launch a nuclear attack. The result is a stable, if terrifying, equilibrium of deterrence sometimes called the balance of terror, in which safety rests on the credible threat of shared annihilation.
mechanism: The doctrine turns not on the size of an arsenal but on its survivability: a retaliatory force that a first strike cannot destroy, so an aggressor cannot disarm its opponent. Survivability is achieved through dispersed, redundant, hard-to-target forces, classically the nuclear triad of submarine-launched missiles, hardened or mobile land-based missiles, and strategic bombers, so no first strike can wipe out all of a nation's nuclear forces at once. Because the credible threat of devastating retaliation always survives, and because mutual vulnerability is what preserves the deterrent, defences against missiles were seen as destabilising, which is why the 1972 ABM Treaty limited them.

examples.text: The 1962 crisis, the closest the Cold War came to nuclear war, is often read as MAD's logic under maximum stress, the shared prospect of mutual catastrophe pushing both leaders toward de-escalation.

Submarines hidden at sea, hardened missile silos, and dispersible bombers together mean no aggressor can plausibly destroy all of a nation's nuclear forces in one strike, preserving the retaliatory threat.
The 1972 US-Soviet treaty sharply limited missile defences precisely to preserve mutual vulnerability, the clearest institutional expression of the doctrine that defences undermine stability.

variants.name: Assured destruction
variants.text: Robert McNamara's 1960s criterion of sizing forces to inflict unacceptable damage even after a surprise first strike, the policy from which the mutual doctrine grew.

variants.name: The destabilising defence
variants.text: The paradox that effective missile defences threaten to unravel deterrence, since a side that could shield itself might believe it could strike first and survive.

whyItMatters: MAD is the standard framework for explaining why the United States and the Soviet Union, despite decades of hostility and vast arsenals, never fought a direct nuclear or full-scale war, the so-called long peace. It remains the baseline logic for thinking about deterrence, force survivability, and the requirements of a second-strike posture, and it provided the conceptual rationale for a generation of arms-control agreements that sought to stabilise, rather than eliminate, the balance of terror.

working.text: build dispersed, redundant forces a first strike cannot destroy, since deterrence rests on assured second strike, not sheer numbers.
recognise that shared defencelessness against retaliation is what keeps both sides cautious, so effective defences are destabilising.
remember the doctrine offers no protection against error, false warning, or miscalculation, which it can turn into catastrophe.

limits: MAD's stability is conditional, and each condition is a vulnerability. It assumes rational decision-makers who value survival, so an irrational or apocalyptic actor breaks the logic. It requires credible, survivable retaliation, and offers no protection against accidental launch, false warning, or crisis miscalculation, which it can turn into total catastrophe. Effective missile defences, limited or tactical nuclear-war concepts, proliferation to more actors, and non-state actors with no territory to hold hostage all challenge it. Critics also argue it is immoral, deliberately holding entire civilian populations hostage, and dangerously dependent on perfect rationality and an unbroken absence of accidents.
misreadings: McNamara did not coin the acronym MAD; he promoted assured destruction as a policy criterion, and the acronym came from a critic, Donald Brennan, who used it derisively to argue the posture was irrational. MAD does not mean simply having many bombs; it specifically requires survivable second-strike forces. Under its logic more missile defence does not make a side safer but destabilises deterrence, which is why the ABM Treaty limited defences on purpose. And it is a strategic condition and analytical framework, not a single formally adopted doctrine, since actual targeting policy shifted over time.
origin: Rooted in Bernard Brodie's 1946 statement of nuclear deterrence, the doctrine took shape under US Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara in the 1960s; the ironic acronym MAD is attributed to the critic Donald Brennan of the Hudson Institute.
